question: When does cane leave its island home and enter the written record of the great civilisations — and what is it, to them?
summary: In this folio sugarcane crosses from the islands to the Asian mainland and, for the first time, into texts. The hybrid canes that suit cooler, drier land arise on the continent, and the first words about the plant come from India, from China's southern fringe and from the Greeks who went east with Alexander ([[te1]], [[b1]], [[th1]], [[th3]]). What the texts show is not an industry but a curiosity: a chewing reed, a syrup allowed to sick monks, a lineage name, and a puzzle for foreign observers who cannot explain where the honey comes from when there are no bees ([[b3]], [[b4]], [[th3]]).

Almost everything in the folio is therefore a *first mention*, and the most important question is what each mention actually proves. The Vedic and Buddhist references are the firmest part; the Chinese linguistic claim, the Hebrew sweet cane, the Persian-Indus link and the very date of śarkarā as 'sugar' are all contested or weak ([[b2]], [[th1]], [[th2]], [[x1]]).

By the end the shape of the future is visible in outline: India as the first place to make sugar products (the lump, guḍa, appears by about 300 BC), medicine and religion as the first uses, and the Greek and Roman world hearing of the reed only at second hand ([[te2]], [[b3]], [[w1]]).

themes.title: The cane becomes a mainland crop
text: Hybrid canes (*S. barberi* in north India, *S. sinense* in south China) make cane growable far from the tropics. The first record of the plant in an Indian text is the Atharvaveda, about 1000 BC; the first sugar product, guḍa, follows by about 300 BC.

themes.title: Sugar's first status: medicine and sacred genealogy
text: In the earliest Indian texts syrup is a medicine for sick monks, and the Buddha's own clan traces its descent from a figure named for the cane. Nothing yet marks sugar as a luxury or a commodity.

themes.title: Seen from outside: puzzled foreigners
text: Nearchus' honey from reeds with no bees is the first Greek account; it comes with Alexander's army, which is why the folio's single event is a military one. Whether the older Near East knew cane at all is doubtful: the Persian link to the Indus is unverified, and honey and dates, not cane, are the sweeteners recorded in Babylonia.

themes.title: Words as evidence
text: Much of this folio's evidence is linguistic, and linguistic evidence is the weakest tier: the cane words of the Yue languages, and śarkarā's move from 'gravel' to sugar, are both disputed in date and direction.

turning_points.text: The Atharvaveda names the cane, and the continental hybrid canes appear.
The monastic code allows syrup to the sick: sugar's first religious status is as medicine.
Alexander's army reaches the Indus, bringing the Greek and Roman reed-honey tradition into being.
Nearchus reports reeds that yield honey without bees: the first Greek description of cane juice.
Guḍa, the first lump sugar, appears in the Vinaya and a Dharmasūtra.

how_to_read: Almost the whole folio sits in *Belief*, *Thought* and *Technology*: that is the evidence we have, not a judgement about where sugar mattered. Read the tier label in each note first, because the CONTESTED entries are as informative about the limits of the evidence as about cane itself.
Nothing here shows trade, production on any scale or cooking; those begin in the next folio.

sources.intro: Evidence for this period is almost entirely secondary: the folio draws on Needham's sugar volume and its Daniels chapters, with Mazumdar and Daniels as the main interpreters. No Sanskrit or Pali text was read in the original.
main: Needham, *Science and Civilisation in China* 6.3 (Daniels and Menzies), for the Indian and Chinese textual record, the hybrid canes and the chronology of sugar products ([[te1]], [[b1]], [[b3]], [[te2]]).
Mazumdar, *Sugar and Society in China*, and Daniels's own studies, for the Chinese side ([[th1]], [[th2]]).
Strabo (Hamilton and Falconer translation, read on Perseus) for Nearchus, the folio's one direct classical source ([[th3]]).
contested: The prophets' 'sweet cane' is most likely an aromatic reed, not sugarcane ([[b2]]).
Benedict's Yue-language cane words, criticised by Bellwood and Pulleyblank ([[th1]]).
When śarkarā came to mean sugar: after 500 BC, or centuries later ([[th2]]).
Persian-Indus contact about sugar is a popular claim without a primary source ([[x1]]).
gaps: The Sanskrit and Pali sources themselves were not read; a specialist on early Indian textual history would settle several datings.
No archaeological evidence for cane processing on the mainland in this period.
